overview: The file chiefly documents mounting Japanese and Manchukuo efforts in 1936–1937 to organize, regulate, censor, and potentially monopolize motion-picture production and distribution in Manchuria and the Kwantung Leased Territory. American consular despatches from Dairen describe pressure on American distributors to join a Japanese association, obstructive customs enforcement, reported Kwantung Army plans for a state-backed monopoly, and the possibility that American companies would withdraw from the market. A translated Japanese trade article supplies detailed plans for a jointly financed film company, propaganda studios near Hsinking, compulsory exhibition, industry statistics, and a catalogue of Manchukuo publicity films. The bundle also contains a sparse filing sheet and an apparently misplaced 1933 State Department memorandum about a Manchu-Japanese economic conference.

subfiles.title: Despatch on difficulties confronting American film distributors in Dairen
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese pressure on American film distributors to join a formal association and related customs impediments in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Japanese distributors sought to create a formal association that could make a collective customs deposit and handle the daily hirage tax. Although the customs commissioner denied requiring membership, Paramount, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, and Fox representatives were warned that business would not proceed smoothly if they remained outside it. Stricter enforcement at the Dairen Custom-house subsequently caused delays and financial losses, while the American firms considered creating an organization modeled on the Tokyo association.

subfiles.title: Filing sheet with April 2 annotation
subfiles.about: Preserves a brief administrative annotation associated with the surrounding correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The page bears the partial date “April 2,” two unidentified image areas, and the phrase “To note marked postage.” It contains no substantive discussion of the motion-picture dispute and appears to be an administrative or routing sheet.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the projected film-distribution monopoly, with Garrels note
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon; appended note by Arthur Garrels
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a Kwantung Army plan to monopolize film distribution and the likelihood that American companies would leave the Manchurian market rather than submit.
subfiles.summary: Foreign distributors had yielded to pressure to join the new association, but Grummon reported a more serious plan by the Kwantung Army to establish a film-distribution monopoly for ideological control and profit. The South Manchuria Railway Company and Kwantung Government were each said to have provided 250,000 yen for an investigation, with foreign suppliers initially compensated according to recent profits but deprived of control over distribution. Grummon warned that American firms might stop supplying films, threatening the viability of more than fifty theaters. In a note dated February 24, Arthur Garrels confirmed that major American distributors meeting in Tokyo were prepared to close their offices and withdraw.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the anticipated scope and timing of the film monopoly
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Relays Major Shibata's account that the proposed monopoly would initially make propaganda shorts and accept films voluntarily before eventually controlling all distribution.
subfiles.summary: An American distributor's inquiries in Harbin and Hsinking produced limited reassurance about the monopoly's immediate scope. Major Shibata said its early work would consist of propaganda shorts and distribution for foreign companies entering voluntarily, although complete control of distribution remained the eventual objective. Films entering from China without Japanese censorship would be closely controlled to restrict Chinese access to outside ideas. The planners still lacked business knowledge and theater data, with only about ten percent of surveyed theaters responding.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting evidence of the proposed Manchukuo film company
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon; appended note by Arthur Garrels
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits Japanese and Chinese press evidence confirming plans for a semi-governmental film company and monopoly in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Grummon summarized a translated article from KEIZAI-MANSHU describing a company capitalized at five million yuan, divided between the Manchukuo Government and the South Manchuria Railway Company. The company would build studios near Hsinking, manufacture propaganda and artistic films, and eventually derive revenue from legal control of distribution and exhibition. Additional press reports said the State Public Information Committee had approved the plan and that investigators were visiting Jilin, Mukden, Harbin, and Dairen. Statements attributed to Kobamatsu explicitly connected government control of film rental and exhibition with modern propaganda policy and the displacement of foreign distributors.

subfiles.title: Translated article, “A Film Producing Company Will Be Established in Manchukuo Shortly”
subfiles.to: Enclosed with Stuart E. Grummon's despatch to the American Embassy in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Details the organization, finances, propaganda mission, studio plans, market statistics, and earlier productions of the proposed Manchukuo film company.
subfiles.summary: The article describes a company promoted by Major Shibano and Japanese film industrialists, licensed by the Manchukuo Government and funded equally by that government and the South Manchuria Railway. Its purposes included promoting “right thoughts,” excluding undesirable foreign ideas, controlling imports and exhibition, and producing exportable artistic films; a large studio site was selected outside Hsinking. The article gives 1936 statistics for imported films, theaters, and audiences and argues that compulsory cultural-film exhibition and monopolization would provide necessary revenue. It concludes with a year-by-year catalogue of government publicity films produced from 1933 through 1936 and subjects planned for 1937.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on the Manchu-Japanese economic conference
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Dairen consul's report on an August 1933 Manchu-Japanese economic conference.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum characterizes the August 15–17 Dairen conference as generally dull and its speeches as offering nothing new in fact or policy. Committee discussions over Manchukuo import duties generated heated disagreements between Japanese representatives and Japanese officials serving Manchukuo, but apparently produced no definite result. The consul also observed that the Manchukuo delegates seemed impressed by orderly conditions in the Kwantung Leased Territory.

interest: The file offers an unusually detailed view of cultural imperialism as both a commercial and political process: pressure through customs administration, semi-official trade organization, censorship, capital investment, and eventual legal monopoly all appear as complementary instruments. Particularly useful is the juxtaposition of confidential American business intelligence with a Japanese-language article that openly presents film as a means of cultivating approved ideas and excluding hostile ones. The enclosure's market statistics and catalogue of Manchukuo publicity productions provide concrete evidence for studying the development of state cinema. The anomalous 1933 economic-conference memorandum and the filing sheet also reveal the sometimes untidy composition of State Department decimal files, while the file title's reference to concerts contrasts with its overwhelmingly cinematic contents.
